tests.description: Malformed JSON is a 400, distinct from a 422 — the body was never understood, so there are no field problems to report.
tests.key: POST /api/contact › answers malformed JSON with 400

tests.description: Validation runs before persistence: an invalid submission must not reach the database, and the sender needs the per-field problems back.
tests.key: POST /api/contact › rejects an invalid submission with 422 and saves nothing

tests.description: A failed write is the one case where the sender must NOT be told it worked: nothing was saved and nothing was sent, so they should retry.
tests.key: POST /api/contact › returns 500 and does not attempt delivery when the write fails

tests.description: The whole point of writing before sending: a mail outage must leave a recoverable row rather than losing the note. So the row is created even when delivery fails, and the sender still gets a success.
tests.key: POST /api/contact › saves the note and still returns 201 when delivery fails

tests.description: The happy path stamps the row, and only after the provider accepted.
tests.key: POST /api/contact › stamps emailedAt once delivery succeeds

tests.description: The note is already safe once the row exists, so a stamping failure must not turn a saved note into a 500 that invites a duplicate submission.
tests.key: POST /api/contact › still returns 201 when stamping fails after a successful send

tests.description: The honeypot must short-circuit BEFORE anything is written, or a bot would fill the table with rows while being told it succeeded.
tests.key: POST /api/contact › writes nothing when the honeypot is tripped

tests.description: Pins the canonical origin's exact shape. Three consumers concatenate onto it — document metadata, robots.txt, sitemap.xml — so a trailing slash here silently becomes "//sitemap.xml" in the advertised sitemap link.
tests.key: SITE_URL › is the bare apex over https, with no trailing slash

tests.description: Guards against canonicalising a host that only redirects. www.nadiaeldeib.com and both forms of nseldeib.com 301 to the apex; naming any of them here would point every crawler and share link at a redirect instead of the real page.
tests.key: SITE_URL › names the apex rather than a redirecting host

tests.description: The plain-text part must be the composed note exactly — it is the copy that survives every client.
tests.key: buildSendPayload › carries the composed note as the plaintext part

tests.description: The HTML part wraps the same text in a <pre> so the line breaks survive, and the note itself must be escaped on the way in.
tests.key: buildSendPayload › escapes the note inside the HTML part

tests.description: Customer.io identifies the recipient as a person in the workspace; on the sandbox tier that identifier is what must be verified for delivery.
tests.key: buildSendPayload › identifies the recipient by the inbox address

tests.description: The subject is how the inbox is scanned, so both facts belong in it.
tests.key: buildSendPayload › puts the topic and the sender in the subject

tests.description: Replying should answer the person who wrote in, not the site's own sending address. This breaks silently — nobody notices until a reply goes nowhere.
tests.key: buildSendPayload › replies to the sender, and delivers to the configured inbox

tests.description: sourcePage is optional; an absent one must not leave a dangling label.
tests.key: composeBody › omits the source line when there is no source page

tests.description: The sender's own words go last and unwrapped, so a long note is not pushed below a wall of metadata.
tests.key: composeBody › puts the metadata first and the message last, verbatim

tests.description: The honeypot reply must be INDISTINGUISHABLE from a real success: same status, same body shape. Any difference tells whoever wrote the bot which field gave them away, and they simply stop filling it in next time.
tests.key: contactResponses › answers a tripped honeypot exactly like a success

tests.description: Unparseable input is the client's problem, not a server fault. A 500 here would tell the sender to try again later when the request will never work.
tests.key: contactResponses › answers unreadable input with 400

tests.description: 201 regardless of whether the email went out — the row exists either way, and delivery is not the sender's problem. The id goes back so a follow-up can reference the note.
tests.key: contactResponses › reports the saved row with a 201

tests.description: 422 rather than 400: the request was understood, the contents were not acceptable. The per-field problems have to survive so the form can point at the field that needs fixing instead of showing a generic failure.
tests.key: contactResponses › returns the field problems with a 422

tests.description: "Nothing was sent" is literally true when the write failed, and it matters: it tells the sender to retry rather than assume the note arrived.
tests.key: contactResponses › says nothing was sent when the write failed

tests.description: The ordering rule. `emailedAt` is the only record of whether a note actually reached the inbox, so stamping it for a send that failed would make an undelivered note indistinguishable from a delivered one.
tests.key: deliverAndStamp › does not stamp when the provider rejects the send

tests.description: The row is already safe by the time this runs, so nothing here is worth failing the request over. A throw would turn a saved note into a 500 and invite the sender to submit it twice.
tests.key: deliverAndStamp › never throws, even when stamping blows up

tests.description: A failed stamp after a successful send is the one acceptable inconsistency: the note arrived but the row still reads as undelivered. Better a duplicate-looking row than a message believed sent that never was.
tests.key: deliverAndStamp › reports delivered-unstamped when the row update fails

tests.description: The operator needs to know which of the two problems occurred, and the provider's own reason is what distinguishes a bad token from an unverified recipient.
tests.key: deliverAndStamp › reports the provider reason on a failed send

tests.description: Sending must happen before stamping, not concurrently — if the write were issued first, a provider rejection would leave a false record behind.
tests.key: deliverAndStamp › sends before it stamps

tests.description: The happy path, and the id must be the saved row's — stamping the wrong row would mark someone else's note as delivered.
tests.key: deliverAndStamp › stamps the saved row once the provider accepts

tests.description: Logging is the caller's business; omitting the hook must not crash the delivery path.
tests.key: deliverAndStamp › works without an onProblem hook

tests.description: A bare status code cannot distinguish a bad token from an unverified recipient, and both are things only the operator can fix.
tests.key: describeSendFailure › includes the status and the provider detail

tests.description: An empty body must not leave a trailing colon with nothing after it.
tests.key: describeSendFailure › omits the separator when there is no detail

tests.description: Reading the body can itself fail; the status is still worth reporting and this must not throw into the delivery path, which promises never to throw.
tests.key: describeSendFailure › still reports the status when the body cannot be read

tests.description: The reason lands in a log line, so a huge HTML error page must not be pasted into it wholesale.
tests.key: describeSendFailure › truncates a long body

tests.description: Ampersand must be escaped FIRST or the escapes themselves get re-escaped into `&lt;`, which renders as visible garbage.
tests.key: escapeHtml › does not double-escape its own output

tests.description: The note is untrusted input interpolated into the HTML part. Without this a message containing markup would alter the email's structure.
tests.key: escapeHtml › escapes the characters that could alter the markup

tests.description: The common case, and the one that must never regress: a real submission that leaves the hidden field alone has to pass straight through.
tests.key: isHoneypotTripped › does not trip for an ordinary submission

tests.description: Whitespace is not content. A stray space injected by an autofill would otherwise silently discard a real person's message — the worst failure this endpoint has, because the sender is told it succeeded.
tests.key: isHoneypotTripped › does not trip on whitespace alone

tests.description: The payload is untrusted, so every shape has to be survivable rather than throwing before validation ever runs.
tests.key: isHoneypotTripped › survives payloads that are not objects

tests.description: `company` is rendered but hidden: a human never fills it, a bot that fills every field does.
tests.key: isHoneypotTripped › trips when the hidden field has content

tests.description: The contact section is last and is a real target, so the final entry must be reachable rather than dropping off the end.
tests.key: pickActive › can return the last section

tests.description: Observer callbacks arrive in whatever order the browser batches them, so the answer must not depend on insertion order of the visible set.
tests.key: pickActive › does not depend on the order ids were added to the set

tests.description: A stale id left in the set by a removed section must not win, or the nav would highlight something that is no longer on the page.
tests.key: pickActive › ignores ids that are not in the ordered list

tests.description: Nothing crosses the band while the hero fills the screen, and the nav indicator is meant to be absent there rather than guessing at a section.
tests.key: pickActive › is null when nothing is visible

tests.description: An empty order is the pre-hydration case: no sections found in the DOM yet.
tests.key: pickActive › is null when there is no ordered list

tests.description: Sections are contiguous, so during a scroll two can briefly both report visible. Document order breaks the tie, which keeps the indicator moving forward instead of flickering back and forth.
tests.key: pickActive › prefers the earliest in document order when several are visible

tests.description: The ordinary case: exactly one section crosses the band.
tests.key: pickActive › returns the one visible section

tests.description: A bare JSON value parses fine. Deciding it is not a usable message is validation's job, not parsing's — conflating the two would answer 400 where the form expects a 422 with field problems.
tests.key: readJsonBody › accepts valid JSON that is not an object

tests.description: The endpoint is public, so malformed input is an expected arrival, not an exceptional one. It must come back as a result the route can answer with a 400 rather than as a thrown error that would surface as a 500.
tests.key: readJsonBody › reports failure instead of throwing on malformed JSON

tests.description: An empty body is the same class of problem and must take the same path.
tests.key: readJsonBody › reports failure on an empty body

tests.description: The ordinary path: a well-formed submission must reach the route as a payload it can hand to validation.
tests.key: readJsonBody › returns the parsed payload for valid JSON

tests.description: The whole point of reporting missing NAMES is that the values must never be logged — CONTACT_INBOX in particular is the address the site exists to keep unpublished.
tests.key: readMailConfig › names every missing variable without revealing any value

tests.description: A partially-configured deployment is the realistic failure — the operator needs to know WHICH one they forgot, not just that something is wrong.
tests.key: readMailConfig › names only the one that is absent

tests.description: The success shape is what the sender destructures, so the three values must come back under the names it expects and unmodified.
tests.key: readMailConfig › returns the config once all three are present

tests.description: An env file with `CONTACT_INBOX=""` left as a placeholder is unconfigured, not configured-to-empty. Treating it as set would send to nowhere.
tests.key: readMailConfig › treats an empty string as unset

tests.description: The message is the entire value of failing fast: it has to name the file the value belongs in, or the reader is no better off than with a stack trace from the driver.
tests.key: requireConnectionString › names where the value belongs

tests.description: A configured environment must pass through untouched — the guard exists to catch absence, not to rewrite a working connection string.
tests.key: requireConnectionString › returns the connection string when it is set

tests.description: Failing here rather than at the first query is the whole point. Postgres has no local-file default, so without this the first symptom is a driver-level error at request time that says nothing about the cause.
tests.key: requireConnectionString › throws when DATABASE_URL is absent

tests.description: A committed env file with `DATABASE_URL=""` left blank is unconfigured. Handing an empty string to the driver produces a confusing connection error instead of the message below.
tests.key: requireConnectionString › treats an empty string as unset

tests.description: The editor's isolation routes already 404 in production. Naming them in a Disallow would publish a list of paths that do not exist — robots.txt is public, so a Disallow advertises a path rather than hiding it.
tests.key: robots › disallows nothing, so it cannot advertise the isolation routes

tests.description: The site is a public personal page with nothing to hide, so the rule must stay fully open. A stray Disallow here would quietly de-index the whole site, which is the single highest-cost mistake this file can make.
tests.key: robots › lets every crawler read the whole site

tests.description: The sitemap must be advertised on the canonical host. Pointing at a redirecting hostname costs a hop on every crawler fetch and muddies which domain owns the content — the exact ambiguity this cycle's redirects exist to remove.
tests.key: robots › points at the sitemap on the canonical host

tests.description: Customer.io's regional hosts are separate deployments and a token issued in one is rejected by the other, so this defaulting is a real failure mode rather than cosmetics.
tests.key: sendUrl › defaults to the US host

tests.description: Anything that is not "eu" must fall back to US rather than building a nonsense host out of an unrecognised value.
tests.key: sendUrl › falls back to US for an unrecognised region

tests.description: Case-insensitive because the value is hand-typed into an env file, and `EU` failing over to the US host would be a 401 with no obvious cause.
tests.key: sendUrl › uses the EU host when the region says so, case-insensitively

tests.description: The ordinary case: a root-relative path appends cleanly. Since SITE_URL has no trailing slash and the path carries a leading one, naive concatenation is already correct here — this locks that in.
tests.key: siteUrl › joins a root-relative path without doubling the slash

tests.description: Sweeps the boundary inputs at once — root, empty, bare, rooted, and nested — to assert the invariant that no combination emits "//" after the origin. A doubled slash yields a URL that resolves but is treated as a distinct address by crawlers.
tests.key: siteUrl › never emits a doubled slash after the origin

tests.description: The site root must render as the bare origin, with no trailing slash, whether it is requested by default or explicitly as '/'. This is the value that lands in the sitemap's <loc> and in og:url.
tests.key: siteUrl › returns the bare origin for the site root

tests.description: A caller that omits the leading slash must not produce "nadiaeldeib.comsitemap.xml". This is the case naive concatenation gets wrong, so it is the reason the helper exists at all rather than a template literal at each call site.
tests.key: siteUrl › tolerates a path given without its leading slash

tests.description: Every <loc> must name the canonical apex. A sitemap listing www. or nseldeib.com would submit redirecting URLs for indexing, splitting the site's identity across hosts — the precise outcome the redirects in this cycle are meant to prevent.
tests.key: sitemap › advertises no host that only redirects

tests.description: With exactly one page, that page is by definition the most important one on the site, so priority must be the maximum.
tests.key: sitemap › gives the only page top priority

tests.description: The site is one page. Its six numbered sections are anchors within '/', not routes, so listing them would hand crawlers several URLs that all resolve to the same document. This fails loudly if someone adds anchors as if they were pages.
tests.key: sitemap › lists the single page the site actually has

tests.description: lastModified must be a real Date, not a string or an Invalid Date. Next serialises it into <lastmod>, and a malformed value there makes crawlers discard the freshness signal for the entry entirely.
tests.key: sitemap › stamps a real lastModified date

tests.description: The brand sitting at either end is a real case: no stray empty segment, and the rendered sentence must be byte-identical to the input.
tests.key: splitOnBrand › handles the brand at the start or the end

tests.description: Matching is case-sensitive on purpose: the brand is a proper noun, and linking a lowercase "codeyam" mid-sentence would be wrong.
tests.key: splitOnBrand › is case-sensitive

tests.description: Reassembly is the real invariant: before + brand + after must reproduce the original exactly, or the footer would quietly change her words.
tests.key: splitOnBrand › reassembles to the original string

tests.description: If the copy is ever edited to drop the brand, the whole string must still render — silently losing the signoff would be worse than not linking it.
tests.key: splitOnBrand › returns the whole string when the brand is absent

tests.description: The footer signoff is one authored string with the brand inside it. The split is what lets the brand become a link without hard-coding the copy.
tests.key: splitOnBrand › splits a sentence around the brand

tests.description: Only the first occurrence is linked. Linking the same word twice in one line reads as a mistake, and the second half must keep its text.
tests.key: splitOnBrand › splits on the first occurrence only

tests.description: Empty inputs must not throw or produce undefined halves, since the result is spread straight into JSX.
tests.key: splitOnBrand › survives empty input

tests.description: JSON from the wire is untrusted: a number, a null, or an object where a string belongs must collapse to empty rather than reach a length check.
tests.key: str › returns empty for a non-string

tests.description: Surrounding whitespace is the difference between a name and a name with a stray paste, so the coercion has to trim before anything else sees it.
tests.key: str › trims a string

tests.description: The request shape is a contract with the route: POST, JSON content type, and sourcePage folded into the body alongside the form values.
tests.key: submitMessage › POSTs JSON to the contact route with sourcePage attached

tests.description: An error response with no readable body still has to produce a message, because the form renders one unconditionally on failure.
tests.key: submitMessage › falls back to a message when the error body is unreadable

tests.description: A server error carries its own copy; the form should show that rather than inventing a message.
tests.key: submitMessage › passes through the server error message on a 500

tests.description: A thrown fetch means the request never landed. That is as likely to be the server as the connection, so the copy must not pick a culprit.
tests.key: submitMessage › reports a failure when fetch throws

tests.description: The happy path. A 201 is the only signal the form uses to swap itself for the confirmation, so it must not be conflated with anything else.
tests.key: submitMessage › reports sent on a 2xx

tests.description: Field problems come back as a 422 and must reach the form as per-field messages, not as a generic failure that discards them.
tests.key: submitMessage › surfaces per-field problems from a 422

tests.description: A 422 with no problems object is a malformed response, not a field error. Treating it as "invalid" would leave the form with nothing to point at.
tests.key: submitMessage › treats a 422 without problems as a failure

tests.description: The delivered count is what makes the seeded undelivered row visible in the output — the state is easy to seed and easy to forget is there.
tests.key: summarize › counts delivered and undelivered separately

tests.description: A clone with no seed file is a valid state, so the summary has to read as a sentence rather than dividing by zero or printing NaN.
tests.key: summarize › reads correctly for an empty set

tests.description: The regression this file exists to prevent: the allow-list was written out by hand and drifted from the chips, so the form's own default selection ("Working together") came back 422 and the note could not be sent.
tests.key: the topic allow-list and the form agree › accepts every topic the form actually offers

tests.description: The default is what someone sends if they never touch the chips, so it has to be valid even more surely than the rest.
tests.key: the topic allow-list and the form agree › accepts the chip the form selects by default

tests.description: The seed file carries ISO strings but Prisma wants Date objects; handing it a string is the mistake this pins.
tests.key: toMessageRow › converts both timestamps when present

tests.description: The two absences mean different things and must not be collapsed: `createdAt` undefined lets the column default apply, while `emailedAt` null is a deliberate value meaning "arrived but never delivered".
tests.key: toMessageRow › distinguishes an absent createdAt from an absent emailedAt

tests.description: An explicit null in the seed file is the undelivered state the fixture exists to represent, and must survive as null rather than becoming a date.
tests.key: toMessageRow › keeps an explicit null emailedAt

tests.description: sourcePage is nullable in the schema; undefined in the fixture must become an explicit null rather than being dropped from the insert.
tests.key: toMessageRow › normalises a missing sourcePage to null

tests.description: The baseline: an ordinary note passes clean and hands back the parsed value, which is what the route persists.
tests.key: validateMessage › accepts a well-formed message

tests.description: Deliberately permissive. Plus-addressing, apostrophes, and subdomains are all real addresses that a clever pattern would turn away.
tests.key: validateMessage › accepts addresses a stricter pattern would wrongly reject

tests.description: Topic is a closed set backing the form's chips. Anything outside it is a forged payload, and an empty topic is the unset case.
tests.key: validateMessage › accepts every listed topic and rejects anything else

tests.description: sourcePage is optional context for triage, so it passes through when sent and becomes an explicit null rather than undefined when it is not.
tests.key: validateMessage › carries sourcePage through, or null when absent

tests.description: The limits guard the column widths. Checking the boundary both ways proves the comparison is not off by one and does not reject a legitimate maximum.
tests.key: validateMessage › enforces the length limits

tests.description: The one thing worth rejecting is an address that cannot receive a reply: no @, nothing either side of it, or a domain with no dot.
tests.key: validateMessage › rejects an address with no @ or no dotted domain

tests.description: The form marks every bad field at once. Bailing on the first problem would walk someone through their mistakes one reload at a time.
tests.key: validateMessage › reports every problem at once, not just the first

tests.description: A note with no name or no reply address cannot be answered, which is the only thing this form exists to make possible.
tests.key: validateMessage › requires a name, an email, and a body

tests.description: A body that is not an object at all must fail as invalid input rather than throwing, so the route can answer 422 instead of 500.
tests.key: validateMessage › survives a non-object payload

tests.description: Spaces and newlines are not content. Without this, a field holding only whitespace passes the truthiness check and stores as blank.
tests.key: validateMessage › treats whitespace-only input as missing

tests.description: Trimming has to happen before validation, not after, or a padded name both passes the empty check and gets stored with its padding.
tests.key: validateMessage › trims every field before validating
